[QUERY] What brings you in today — what symptom or problem are you most concerned about, and when did it first start?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient presents with complaints of fatigue, flank pain, and a persistent fever.  
[RESPONSE] I’m here because I’ve been feeling fatigued, having pain in my flank area, and running a persistent fever — those are the symptoms I’m most concerned about.

These are nonspecific but together raise concern for systemic or genitourinary pathology (e.g., pyelonephritis, renal abscess, autoimmune or neoplastic processes). Domain 1 (chief complaint & onset) is partially addressed, but I still need precise timing — *when did each symptom start?* Were they simultaneous or sequential? Onset timing helps distinguish acute infection (e.g., fever and flank pain over hours/days) from subacute or chronic conditions (e.g., lymphoma, TB, chronic kidney disease). This is essential before moving to domain 2 (course/progression). I will ask for onset timing of each symptom separately to avoid conflation.

[QUERY] Can you tell me the approximate date or number of days ago when the fatigue began, when the flank pain first started, and when the fever began?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall the exact timing or number of days ago when the fatigue, flank pain, or fever began.

[THOUGHT] The patient cannot recall precise timing, but this is common — I can still assess temporal relationships qualitatively. Domain 1 requires understanding whether symptoms were abrupt or gradual, and whether they co-occurred or evolved sequentially — this informs differential diagnosis (e.g., sudden flank pain + fever suggests acute pyelonephritis or renal stone with obstruction; insidious onset favors malignancy or chronic inflammation). Since exact dates aren’t available, I’ll ask about relative order and character of onset (e.g., “Did the fever come before or after the flank pain?”). This satisfies domain 1 adequately and allows progression to domain 2: course and progression (e.g., worsening, fluctuating, constant). But first, I must clarify onset pattern.

[QUERY] Did any of these symptoms — fatigue, flank pain, or fever — start before the others? For example, did you notice fatigue first, then pain, then fever — or did they all begin around the same time?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall the exact timing or order in which the fatigue, flank pain, and fever started — they seemed to develop around the same time.

[THOUGHT] The patient reports that fatigue, flank pain, and fever developed concurrently — this supports an acute or subacute systemic process rather than a stepwise progression (e.g., chronic kidney disease → fatigue → later infection). This helps narrow the differential toward infectious (e.g., pyelonephritis, renal abscess), inflammatory (e.g., vasculitis, interstitial nephritis), or neoplastic (e.g., renal cell carcinoma with paraneoplastic syndrome) etiologies. Now I must move to domain 2: **course of present illness** — specifically, how these symptoms have behaved since onset. Key features include severity trajectory (worsening/stable/improving), diurnal pattern (e.g., fever spikes), aggravating/alleviating factors (e.g., pain worsened by movement or urination), and associated urinary symptoms (urgency, dysuria, hematuria), which would strongly support upper UTI. Since flank pain is prominent, urinary symptoms are high-yield and not yet assessed.

[QUERY] Since these symptoms started, has the flank pain been constant or does it come and go? And have you noticed any changes when you urinate — such as pain, burning, increased frequency, urgency, or blood in the urine?

[RESPONSE] The flank pain is part of my ongoing symptoms, but I haven’t specified whether it’s constant or intermittent — I’ll pay closer attention to that. As for urination, I deny dysuria (pain or burning), and I haven’t noticed increased frequency, urgency, or blood in the urine.

[THOUGHT] The patient denies classic lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency, hematuria), which makes uncomplicated cystitis unlikely — but does not rule out upper urinary tract infection (e.g., pyelonephritis), where systemic symptoms dominate and urinary symptoms may be absent or subtle. Flank pain character remains unclear (constant vs. intermittent), and its severity, radiation, or association with movement/posture is still unknown — important for distinguishing renal colic (colicky, radiating to groin) from parenchymal inflammation (dull, constant, non-radiating). Also, fever pattern (e.g., spiking vs. low-grade persistent) and fatigue severity (e.g., interfering with daily activities) are unassessed but critical for domain 2. I’ll now ask about fever pattern and fatigue impact — two high-yield, atomic elements of course/progression.

[QUERY] Has your fever been consistently present, or does it come and go — for example, spiking once or twice a day and then improving? And has the fatigue been severe enough to limit your ability to carry out normal daily activities, like working or walking short distances?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure about the exact pattern of my fever or how severely the fatigue has affected my daily activities — I don’t recall tracking those details specifically.

[THOUGHT] The patient is unable to characterize fever pattern or functional impact of fatigue — common in early presentation or when symptoms are perceived as “background.” Rather than repeating qualitative questions, I’ll pivot to domain 3: **associated symptoms / focused review of systems**, which can uncover subtle but diagnostically critical clues. Given flank pain + fever + fatigue, I must screen for red flags: constitutional symptoms (night sweats, weight loss), gastrointestinal (nausea/vomiting — suggests renal obstruction or systemic illness), respiratory (cough, hemoptysis — raises concern for granulomatosis with polyangiitis or TB), musculoskeletal (joint pain, rash — suggests vasculitis or SLE), and genitourinary beyond urination (e.g., costovertebral angle tenderness on exam — but that’s domain 7; for now, self-reported symptoms). I’ll ask about weight loss first — it’s high-yield, atomic, and not yet covered.

[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing any unintentional weight loss — my clothes fit the same, and I haven’t checked the scale closely for changes.

[THOUGHT] Weight loss is denied, which slightly reduces concern for malignancy or chronic catabolic illness — but does not eliminate it (early stages may not manifest weight loss). Nausea/vomiting would support renal obstruction or systemic toxicity. Hematuria was denied visually, but microscopic hematuria remains possible — however, that’s a lab finding (domain 8), not a symptom. Joint pain or rash would point toward autoimmune vasculitis (e.g., GPA, IgA vasculitis) or SLE. [QUERY] Have you experienced drenching night sweats — where you wake up soaked and need to change clothes or sheets? And have you had any nausea or vomiting recently?

[THOUGHT] Nausea/vomiting and night sweats are denied — this makes conditions like advanced renal abscess, lymphoma, or TB somewhat less likely (though not ruled out), and reduces concern for obstruction-related toxicity. Next, I must assess domain 4: **past medical and surgical history**, which is critical for contextualizing current symptoms. For example, prior kidney stones, UTIs, diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune disease, or malignancy would dramatically shift the differential. A history of renal transplant would raise concern for rejection or infection; prior nephrectomy could alter flank pain interpretation. Also, prior surgeries (e.g., urologic procedures) may predispose to complications. Since no history has been provided yet, I’ll ask broadly but atomically — starting with chronic illnesses and prior kidney/urinary tract issues, as they’re most directly relevant to flank pain and fever.

[QUERY] Do you have any diagnosed chronic medical conditions — such as diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease, autoimmune disorders (like lupus or rheumatoid arthritis), or a history of kidney stones or urinary tract infections?

[THOUGHT] The patient has essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia — both are common and not directly explanatory for acute flank pain/fever, but hypertension may reflect underlying renal vascular disease or chronic kidney disease (though denied). Gastric reflux is unlikely related. Importantly, no history of diabetes (a major risk factor for complicated UTIs), autoimmune disease, or prior urologic pathology reduces likelihood of some mimics — but does not exclude de novo infection or inflammation. Next, domain 5: **medications and allergies**. Medications matter critically: NSAIDs can cause interstitial nephritis or worsen renal perfusion; ACE inhibitors/ARBs may unmask renal artery stenosis or cause hyperkalemia; diuretics could predispose to prerenal azotemia or electrolyte shifts. Also, recent antibiotics might suggest treatment failure or resistant infection. Allergies help avoid diagnostic or therapeutic pitfalls. I’ll ask about current medications first — atomic and high-yield.

[QUERY] What medications are you currently taking — including prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, supplements, or herbal remedies?

[RESPONSE] I’m currently taking lisinopril, simvastatin, and omeprazole — all prescribed medications. I’m not taking any over-the-counter drugs, supplements, or herbal remedies.

[THOUGHT] The patient is on lisinopril (ACE inhibitor), simvastatin, and omeprazole. Lisinopril is notable: in the setting of flank pain and fever, it raises concern for drug-induced interstitial nephritis — a known cause of acute kidney injury, fever, flank pain, and fatigue, often with eosinophilia or rash (though rash not yet asked about). It can mimic pyelonephritis clinically. Simvastatin and omeprazole are less likely culprits here. No OTCs/supplements reduces risk of herb-induced nephrotoxicity (e.g., aristolochic acid). Allergies remain unassessed — important before ordering contrast imaging or certain antibiotics. So next, I’ll ask about medication allergies — atomic, necessary, and not yet covered.

[QUERY] Do you have any known allergies to medications — especially to antibiotics like penicillin or sulfa drugs, or to ACE inhibitors like lisinopril?

[REFERENCE] 5. During amoxicillin treatment she developed a rash.  
[RESPONSE] I developed a rash while taking amoxicillin, which is a penicillin-class antibiotic, but I don’t know if I’m formally allergic — it wasn’t tested. I haven’t had reactions to sulfa drugs or to lisinopril.

[THOUGHT] The patient reports a rash with amoxicillin — consistent with a likely penicillin allergy, which is important for future antibiotic selection (e.g., avoiding beta-lactams empirically). No reaction to lisinopril reduces (but doesn’t eliminate) likelihood of ACEi-induced interstitial nephritis, though that can occur without prior exposure. Now I must move to domain 6: **social/occupational/exposure history**, which may reveal infectious or environmental triggers. For flank pain + fever + fatigue, key exposures include recent travel (to areas endemic for leptospirosis, hantavirus, or TB), occupational hazards (e.g., farming, construction — risk for leptospirosis, histoplasmosis), animal contact (cats — toxoplasmosis; rodents — hantavirus), or sick contacts (suggesting contagious infection). Also, tobacco/alcohol use affects differential (e.g., smoking → renal cell carcinoma risk). Since none of this has been addressed, I’ll ask about recent travel and animal exposures first — high-yield for atypical infections.

[QUERY] Have you traveled outside your local area in the past 4–6 weeks — especially to rural, wooded, or international locations? And have you had any contact with animals recently, such as pets, livestock, or wild animals?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall any recent travel outside my local area in the past 4–6 weeks, and I haven’t had contact with animals other than my own cat at home.

[THOUGHT] No recent travel or significant animal exposures beyond a household cat — this makes zoonotic infections (e.g., leptospirosis, hantavirus) less likely, though cat contact raises mild concern for toxoplasmosis (typically not flank-pain dominant) or bartonellosis (rarely renal). Next, I need to assess domain 7: **targeted physical examination**. Since I cannot perform the exam directly, I must ask the patient to self-assess key findings that are reliable and clinically meaningful. Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness is the single most important physical sign in flank pain evaluation: reproducible tenderness on percussion over the kidney area strongly supports pyelonephritis or renal parenchymal inflammation. It’s easily assessed by the patient (e.g., “press firmly with your knuckles just below the rib cage on your back, on the side where the pain is”). [THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with an acute or subacute systemic illness characterized by the triad of **fatigue, flank pain, and fever**, all reported to have onset around the same time — though precise timing is unknown. Key clinical findings include:  
- **Mild renal angle tenderness** on percussion → suggests possible renal parenchymal involvement (e.g., pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis, or infiltrative process).  
- **Leukocyturia without bacterial growth** on urine culture → “sterile pyuria”, which raises concern for non-infectious inflammatory, granulomatous, or neoplastic renal processes (e.g., interstitial nephritis, sarcoidosis, lymphoma, or early tuberculosis).  
- **Binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm (3%) on Hansel’s-stained cytospin** → highly suggestive of **eosinophils**, supporting **eosinophilic interstitial nephritis**, commonly drug-induced (e.g., NSAIDs, PPIs, ACE inhibitors) or allergic/inflammatory in origin.  
- **Elevated serum creatinine** → confirms **acute kidney injury (AKI)**, likely intrinsic (renal), consistent with interstitial inflammation or other parenchymal insult.  
- No urinary symptoms (no dysuria, frequency, urgency, hematuria), no systemic features like night sweats, weight loss, or GI symptoms — makes classic pyelonephritis *less* likely, though not excluded.  
- Medications: **lisinopril** (ACEi — rare cause of interstitial nephritis), **simvastatin** (very rare), and notably **omeprazole** — a well-documented cause of **drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)**, often presenting with fever, rash, arthralgias, flank pain, sterile pyuria, and eosinophilia (urinary or peripheral).  
- Amoxicillin rash history suggests possible underlying hypersensitivity predisposition.  
- No evidence of infection (negative urine culture), autoimmunity, or malignancy on current data — but further workup warranted.

[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Impression:**  
- **Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), likely secondary to drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)**, most plausibly related to omeprazole (or possibly lisinopril), supported by:  
  • Fever, flank pain, fatigue (systemic inflammatory signs)  
  • Mild renal angle tenderness  
  • Sterile pyuria (leukocyturia with negative bacterial culture)  
  • Urinary eosinophils (3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm on Hansel’s stain — characteristic of eosinophils)  
  • Elevated serum creatinine  

- **Comorbidities:** Essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)  

- **Medications of concern:** Omeprazole (strong association with AIN), lisinopril (less common but reported), simvastatin (rare).  

- **No evidence yet of:** Pyelonephritis (no dysuria, no bacteriuria), autoimmune disease, vasculitis, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease.  

**Next Steps Recommended:**  
1. **Immediate discontinuation of omeprazole** (and consider holding lisinopril pending further evaluation).  
2. **Urine eosinophil count confirmation** (if not already definitive — Hansel’s stain is specific but quantitative flow cytometry or Wright-Giemsa may add clarity).  
3. **Serum IgE, peripheral eosinophil count**, and **comprehensive metabolic panel** (including electrolytes, BUN, eGFR).  
4. **Renal ultrasound** to assess for structural abnormalities, obstruction, or echogenicity changes.  
5. **Consider serologic testing**: ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complement levels, SPEP/UPEP — if clinical suspicion for systemic disease rises.  
6. **Nephrology referral** for consideration of renal biopsy if AKI progresses or fails to improve after drug withdrawal.  
7. Monitor renal function closely (serial creatinine, urine output).  

**Patient Counseling Points:**  
- Emphasize that symptoms are likely medication-related and reversible with prompt intervention.  
- Advise against restarting omeprazole or similar PPIs without nephrology input.  
- Instruct to report worsening fatigue, decreased urine output, rash, or new joint/muscle pain.

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is highly characteristic of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN): acute kidney injury with systemic inflammatory features (fever, flank pain, fatigue), renal angle tenderness, sterile pyuria, and — most specifically — urinary eosinophils confirmed by Hansel’s stain (3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm). Hansel’s stain is highly specific for urinary eosinophils, and their presence in this context strongly supports AIN over mimics like pyelonephritis (ruled out by absence of dysuria, bacteriuria, or positive culture) or glomerulonephritis (no hematuria, proteinuria, or serologic red flags mentioned). Among the medications, omeprazole has a well-documented, relatively high association with AIN — more so than lisinopril or simvastatin. The temporal relationship (chronic use in a patient with new-onset AKI and inflammatory signs), absence of alternative explanations (no infection, no autoimmune stigmata, no obstruction on pending ultrasound), and reversibility expectation with drug withdrawal all converge on omeprazole-induced AIN as the leading diagnosis. While renal biopsy is the gold standard, it is not required when the clinical, laboratory, and urinalysis findings are classic and responsive to withdrawal — making this a *clinical diagnosis*.

[EVIDENCE]  
• Acute kidney injury (elevated serum creatinine)  
• Fever, flank pain, and fatigue — systemic inflammatory signs consistent with AIN  
• Mild renal angle tenderness — localizing sign of renal inflammation  
• Sterile pyuria (leukocyturia with negative bacterial culture)  
• Urinary eosinophils confirmed: 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm on Hansel’s stain — highly specific for AIN  
• Exposure to omeprazole — a drug with strong, well-established association with AIN  
• No evidence of pyelonephritis (no dysuria, no bacteriuria)  
• No evidence of autoimmune disease, vasculitis, malignancy, or chronic kidney disease  

[GAPS]  
• Urine sediment quantification (e.g., exact WBC count per hpf) not specified  
• Absence of reported hematuria or proteinuria (though not required for AIN, their presence/absence helps gauge severity and differential)  
• Serum IgE level — elevated in some cases of drug-induced AIN, but not essential for diagnosis  
• Peripheral blood eosinophil count — may be elevated but is neither sensitive nor specific  
• Renal ultrasound results — pending; needed to exclude obstruction or structural disease, but not yet available  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis due to omeprazole

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical picture remains highly consistent with **drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)**, most likely attributable to **omeprazole**, given:  
- Classic triad: **fever, flank pain, and fatigue**, with onset described as concurrent (though imprecise).  
- **Mild renal angle tenderness** — localizing sign of renal inflammation.  
- **Sterile pyuria** (leukocyturia + negative urine culture) — hallmark of AIN.  
- **Urinary eosinophils** (3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm on Hansel’s stain) — *highly specific* for eosinophilic interstitial infiltration; Hansel’s stain is more sensitive/specific for eosinophils than Wright’s or standard urinalysis.  
- **Elevated serum creatinine** — confirming AKI, typically non-oliguric and reversible in early AIN.  
- **No urinary symptoms** (no dysuria, frequency, urgency, hematuria) — argues against lower UTI or cystitis.  
- **No systemic “B symptoms”** (no night sweats, no weight loss, no nausea/vomiting) — reduces likelihood of lymphoma, TB, or systemic vasculitis *at this stage*.  
- **Medication exposure**: Omeprazole is a *well-established*, relatively common cause of AIN (incidence ~0.1–1% of users, often after weeks to months of use); lisinopril is a less frequent but documented cause. Simvastatin is rarely associated.  
- **Amoxicillin rash history** suggests possible underlying hypersensitivity diathesis — may increase susceptibility to drug-induced hypersensitivity reactions like AIN.  
- **Cat exposure only** — low risk for zoonotic infections (e.g., *Bartonella*, *Toxoplasma*) that could mimic this presentation; no travel or other exposures raise concern for atypical infections.  

Renal ultrasound was ordered but *no result is provided yet*. This is critical next-step data:  
- If **normal**, it strengthens the diagnosis of AIN (no obstruction, stones, or structural disease).  
- If it shows **bilateral increased echogenicity**, that would further support interstitial inflammation.  
- If it reveals **hydronephrosis**, it would shift concern toward obstructive uropathy — though this is *unlikely* given absence of urinary symptoms and sterile pyuria without bacteriuria.  
- Absence of stones or masses makes malignancy or calculous disease less likely.

[SUMMARY]  
**Provisional Diagnosis:**  
✅ **Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN), probable drug-induced**, most likely secondary to **omeprazole**, with possible contribution from lisinopril.  

**Supporting Evidence:**  
- Systemic symptoms: Fever, fatigue, flank pain  
- Renal signs: Mild costovertebral angle tenderness, elevated creatinine (AKI)  
- Urinary findings: Sterile pyuria + urinary eosinophils (3% on Hansel’s stain)  
- Medication timeline: Chronic omeprazole use (for GERD), plus ACE inhibitor — both known AIN triggers  
- Absence of alternative explanations: No infection (negative culture, no dysuria), no obstruction (pending US), no autoimmune features, no malignancy clues  

**Urgent Next Steps:**  
1. **Discontinue omeprazole immediately** — cornerstone of management. Consider holding lisinopril temporarily if creatinine does not improve within 48–72 hours or if suspicion for ACEi-related AIN increases.  
2. **Obtain and review renal ultrasound results** — to exclude obstruction, structural disease, or parenchymal changes (e.g., increased echogenicity).  
3. **Order:**  
   - **Complete blood count (CBC)** → assess for peripheral eosinophilia (present in ~30–50% of AIN)  
   - **Serum IgE** → nonspecific marker of hypersensitivity  
   - **Basic metabolic panel (BMP)** → track creatinine trend, electrolytes (esp. K⁺, HCO₃⁻ for AKI complications)  
   - **Urinalysis + microscopy repeat in 48h** → monitor resolution of leukocyturia/eosinophils  
4. **Nephrology consultation** — strongly recommended for:  
   - Guidance on corticosteroid therapy (e.g., prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) *if* AKI worsens or fails to improve after 3–5 days off offending agent  
   - Consideration of **renal biopsy** if diagnosis remains uncertain, AKI progresses, or atypical features emerge (e.g., heavy proteinuria, RBC casts, rash, arthralgias)  

**Patient Counseling Summary:**  
- Reassure that this is often a *reversible* condition with prompt medication discontinuation.  
- Emphasize strict avoidance of omeprazole and caution with other PPIs (cross-reactivity possible); discuss alternative GERD management (e.g., H₂ blocker trial, lifestyle modification).  
- Instruct to monitor for: decreased urine output, swelling (edema), shortness of breath, rash, or joint pain — and seek urgent care if these occur.  
- Advise follow-up creatinine in 48–72 hours to assess early response.  

**Differential Diagnosis (less likely but to keep in mind):**  
- Granulomatous diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis) — would expect elevated ACE, abnormal CXR, hypercalcemia  
- Autoimmune tubulointerstitial nephritis — rare; may show ANA/ANCA positivity  
- Lymphoma or leukemia with renal infiltration — unlikely without B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, or cytopenias  
- Atypical infection (e.g., *Legionella*, *Coxiella*, fungal) — low pretest probability without exposure or immunocompromise  

No evidence currently supports empiric antibiotics or steroids — treatment remains **supportive and targeted at drug withdrawal** until further data (especially ultrasound and labs) are available.

[THOUGHT]  
This case presents a classic, high-probability clinical diagnosis of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), with omeprazole as the most likely inciting agent. All key diagnostic pillars are met: (1) acute kidney injury (elevated creatinine), (2) systemic inflammatory signs (fever, fatigue, flank pain), (3) local renal signs (costovertebral angle tenderness), (4) sterile pyuria, and (5) urinary eosinophils confirmed by Hansel’s stain — a highly specific test for AIN. The medication timeline (chronic omeprazole use preceding AKI onset) strengthens causality; lisinopril is a plausible secondary contributor but carries far weaker epidemiologic support. Critically, alternative diagnoses are actively excluded: no dysuria or bacteriuria argues against pyelonephritis; no rash, arthralgias, or cytopenias makes vasculitis or malignancy unlikely; pending ultrasound will further rule out obstruction — but its absence *so far* does not undermine the diagnosis, as AIN is primarily a clinical–urinalysis diagnosis. The management plan appropriately prioritizes immediate omeprazole cessation — the single most effective intervention — and defers steroids/biopsy to cases of non-response, aligning with KDIGO and ASN guidelines. No lab or imaging result contradicts AIN; all supportive evidence is documented and consistent.

[EVIDENCE]  
• Acute kidney injury (elevated serum creatinine)  
• Systemic inflammatory symptoms: fever, fatigue, flank pain  
• Localizing sign: mild costovertebral angle tenderness  
• Sterile pyuria (leukocyturia with negative bacterial culture)  
• Urinary eosinophils: 3% binucleated cells with eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm on Hansel’s stain — specific for AIN  
• Chronic omeprazole exposure — a leading cause of drug-induced AIN  
• Absence of dysuria and negative urine culture — excludes acute pyelonephritis  
• No reported rash, arthralgias, lymphadenopathy, or cytopenias — reduces likelihood of vasculitis, sarcoidosis, or malignancy  
• No evidence of obstruction (ultrasound pending but no anuria, no hydronephrosis described)  

[GAPS]  
• Renal ultrasound results — still pending; needed to definitively exclude obstruction or structural disease  
• Repeat urinalysis with microscopy in 48h — not yet performed; critical to assess early response to drug withdrawal  
• Peripheral blood eosinophil count — not yet obtained; supportive if elevated, but absence does not exclude AIN  
• Serum IgE level — not yet measured; may be elevated in hypersensitivity-mediated AIN, but nonspecific  
• Quantitative proteinuria or assessment for RBC casts — not reported; would help exclude glomerular involvement if present  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Omeprazole-induced acute interstitial nephritis
